GK-10.c01: At night you see hazards later, so you have **less time to react**, and a surprised driver is less able to avoid a crash.
Night driving problems come from three places: **the driver, the roadway, and the vehicle**.
GK-10.c02: Wear corrective lenses **every time** you drive, keep a spare pair, and **never wear dark or tinted lenses at night** because they block light you need.
Glare can blind you briefly, and recovery can take **several seconds**; even **2 seconds** at 55 mph covers more than half a football field.
Fatigue risk is highest **at night**, especially after midnight, and mid-afternoon; **6 hours of sleep or less** triples your risk.
Adults need **8–9 hours** of sleep; on long trips take a break about every **100 miles or 2 hours**.
Caffeine and drugs don't fix drowsiness; **nothing is safe except leaving the road and sleeping** (or a 15–20 minute nap).
GK-10.c03: Many night crashes involve **pedestrians, bicyclists and animals**, who are hard to see on poorly lit roads.
When lighting is poor or confusing, slow down so you can **stop within the distance you can see ahead**.
Be extra alert for drunk drivers around **bar and tavern closing times**.
GK-10.c04: Low beams let you see about **250 ft**; high beams about **350–500 ft**. Keep your stopping distance within your sight distance.
At 55 mph a truck needs at least **419 ft** to stop, far beyond low-beam range; at 35 mph it needs about 222 ft.
Dirty headlights may give only **half** their light; keep all lights, reflectors, signals and the windshield (inside and outside) clean.
[CA] Headlights on from **½ hour after sunset to ½ hour before sunrise**, when using wipers, or when you can't clearly see a person or vehicle 1,000 ft away.
[CA] **Never drive with only parking lights on**.
GK-10.c05: Dim high beams when an oncoming vehicle **or** a vehicle you are following is within **500 ft** (answer 500 ft on the test).
Use high beams whenever it is **safe and legal**; driving on low beams all the time badly shortens your view.
For oncoming glare, look **slightly to the right** at the lane or edge line, and never retaliate with your own high beams.
Keep the cab dark (dome light off), wear **no sunglasses at night**, and stop at the nearest safe place if you get sleepy.
GK-10.c06: Best advice is **don't drive in fog**; pull into a rest area or truck stop and wait for better visibility.
If you must drive, **slow down before** entering fog and use **low beams and fog lights**, even in daytime.
Turn on your **4-way flashers**, use roadside reflectors to see curves, listen for traffic, and avoid passing.
Don't stop on the roadside unless you must, and don't assume lights ahead show where the road is.
GK-10.c07: Winter tread depth: **front tires 4/32 inch** or more in each major groove; **all other tires 2/32 inch** or more.
Carry the right number of **tire chains plus extra cross-links**, check they fit the drive tires, and practice putting them on.
Check coolant/antifreeze, defrosters, wipers with **washer antifreeze**, and clear ice from windows, mirrors, steps and radiator shutters.
Don't set the winterfront too tight, or the engine can **overheat and quit**.
Check the exhaust for leaks, because **carbon monoxide** in the cab causes sleepiness and can kill.
GK-10.c08: On slippery roads be **slow and smooth**; if it is extremely slippery, pull off at the first safe spot.
Check for ice on **bridges and overpasses**; **no spray** from other tires means ice has formed, and ice on mirrors or wipers means the road is probably icy.
**Don't use the engine brake or speed retarder** on slippery roads, because they can make the drive wheels skid.
Melting ice makes the road **even more slippery**; don't brake in curves and keep a longer following distance.
Wet brakes: shift to a low gear, brake **gently**, drive through with light pressure, then dry them and make a **test stop**.
GK-10.c09: In very hot weather inspect tires **every 2 hours or every 100 miles**; **never let air out** of hot tires.
If a tire is **too hot to touch**, stay stopped until it cools, or it may blow out or catch fire.
Keep the **radiator cap closed until the system cools**; a cap cool enough to touch bare-handed is probably safe to open.
Without a recovery tank, turn the cap **slowly to the first stop**, step back, and remove it only after the pressure is gone.
A **slack belt** can't drive the water pump or fan, so the engine overheats; burst hoses can wreck the engine or start a fire.
GK-10.c10: Watch for **bleeding tar**, which rises to the road surface in very hot weather and is **very slippery**.
Drive slowly enough to prevent overheating, because speed raises the risk of **tire failure, fire, and engine failure**.
